results.title: Application of medical gases in prevention and treatment of electromagnetic radiation injury.
results.abstract: The widespread proliferation of electromagnetic technologies in communications, healthcare, and daily life poses increasing risks of radiation-induced tissue injury. Mitigating these deleterious effects remains a formidable challenge. Recently, medical gases, including molecular hydrogen (H2), hydrogen sulfide (H2S), carbon monoxide (CO), nitric oxide (NO), and hyperbaric oxygen, have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality with radioprotective potential. These gases exert their effects through integrated, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial-protective mechanisms. Specifically, the endogenous gasotransmitters (CO, NO, and H2S) modulate precise signaling networks, while the exogenous interventions (H2, and hyperbaric oxygen) function primarily through direct radical scavenging or the induction of hormetic stress responses. This review evaluates the research progress of these five medical gases in preventing and treating injuries across the electromagnetic spectrum. H2 possesses the broadest evidence base, particularly in radiofrequency and ultraviolet protection. H2S and CO demonstrate potent efficacy in addressing ultraviolet-induced skin and retinal damage. NO plays a dual role as both a cytoprotectant and a mediator of bystander effect propagation. Hyperbaric oxygen enhances systemic resilience through preconditioning. Delivery strategies have evolved from conventional inhalation and oral administration toward smart nanocarriers and stimuli-responsive donor systems. However, these platforms still face challenges in spatiotemporal control and long-term safety. Furthermore, broader limitations, including an uneven research distribution across electromagnetic wavebands, a scarcity of clinical trials, and the lack of non-invasive methods for real-time gas concentration monitoring, are comprehensively discussed.

results.title: Experimental evidence for the beneficial effects of low-concentration ozone.
results.abstract: Ozone (O3), a molecule consisting of three oxygen atoms, is an unstable compound whose clinical application as a complementary therapy continues to expand. Although numerous clinical studies support its therapeutic potential, the molecular basis of its effects has remained poorly understood. This review summarizes the current knowledge on the cellular and molecular mechanisms activated by low-concentration O3. Central to its action is the induction of mild oxidative stress by low concentrations of O3, which triggers an antioxidant response mediated through nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2, enhancing cell survival. Additionally, low-concentration O3 exhibits antiinflammatory properties by modulating cytokine expression, inhibiting metalloproteinases, and activating macrophages. The regenerative potential of low-concentration O3 may be attributed to the stimulation of fibroblasts, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts. Moreover, the antitumor effects of low-concentration O3 in cancer cell lines and animal models appear to be linked to the inhibition of cell proliferation and migration, as well as proapoptotic activity. More research is needed to determine the best treatment methods, long-term effectiveness, and standardized clinical procedures for ozone therapy in specific diseases. This review provides a detailed reference for understanding how O3 therapy works.

results.title: A Species‐Dependent Spatial Patterning of FOXP1 and nNOS Protein Expression in the Adult Mammalian Subthalamic Nucleus
results.abstract: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a key component of basal ganglia circuitry involved in motor, cognitive, and limbic functions. While the transcription factor FOXP1 has been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and basal ganglia function, its expression in the adult STN remains insufficiently characterized. Our study investigated the expression and distribution of FOXP1 protein and its colocalization with neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) and a pan-neuronal marker (HuC/HuD) in the adult STN across three mammalian species: mouse, rat, and human. Using immunofluorescent double-labeling and quantitative analysis, we examined their spatial organization and relative proportions within the neuronal population. FOXP1 was identified as a substantial neuronal subpopulation, comprising approximately 40%-45% of STN neurons across all species. In contrast, nNOS-positive neurons showed marked interspecies variation, increasing from ∼32% in mice to ∼68% in humans. Notably, the spatial distribution of these markers differed significantly between species. In rodents, FOXP1+ and nNOS+ neurons were largely segregated along the dorsoventral axis, forming visibly distinct subdomains. Conversely, in the human STN, these populations were diffusely intermixed with a higher degree of colocalization. Additionally, both markers exhibited species-specific antero-posterior gradients. These findings provide the first evidence of FOXP1 protein expression in the adult rat and human STN and highlight fundamental interspecies differences in neuronal organization. The expanded nNOS+ population and increased FOXP1/nNOS colocalization in humans suggest evolutionary divergence in the mammalian STN cytoarchitecture. Overall, the results challenge simplified models of STN subdivision in mammals, primates especially, and underscore the need for caution when extrapolating rodent data to human neurophysiology.

results.title: Alterations in phototransduction timing, dark adaptation and GNAT1 trafficking in GNAT1 -edited Xenopus laevis.
results.abstract: GNAT1 (also called α-transducin) is the α-subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein present in rod photoreceptors that plays a critical role in phototransduction. Photoactivated rhodopsin binds GNAT1, which stimulates phosphodiesterase to hydrolyze cGMP, closing ion channels and hyperpolarizing the rod cell. To examine the effects of GNAT1 ablation on light-induced autophagy and light-exacerbated retinal degeneration, we previously generated genetically chimeric, GNAT1- edited Xenopus laevis using CRISPR technology. Here, we interbred these F0 animals to produce F1 animals with defined genotypes, including full knockouts, and characterized the F1 generation by Western blot, histology, and electroretinography (ERG). In X. laevis tadpoles with nonsense mutations in all four GNAT1 alleles, the GNAT1 protein was absent, and the scotopic ERG was absent, indicating full knockout. In animals with reduced GNAT1 expression, we observed increased A- and B-wave implicit times. Greater GNAT1 protein reduction was associated with greater ERG delay, demonstrating a role for GNAT1 in the timing of phototransduction. We also identified two unexpected phenotypes linked to distinct gene edits. The Q184L- GNAT1.L mutation conferred an ERG phenotype similar to that of a full knockout, but with minimal reduction in GNAT1 protein levels, consistent with loss of function. This mutation is also present in the human population. A three-base-pair deletion (T183,Q184→K183) in GNAT1.S caused dominantly inherited diminished ERG response and defective dark adaptation, and was associated with photoreceptor structural abnormalities and GNAT1 accumulation at the connecting cilium, consistent with a dominant-negative effect on GNAT1 trafficking.

results.title: Anatomy and Function
results.abstract: The liver is derived from a foregut endodermal bud, which develops in the third week of gestation and divides into two parts: hepatic and biliary. The lobule described by Kiernan is the most widely used unit of liver microanatomy, consisting of a hexagon-like region of liver parenchyma with a central vein as its hub and portal tracts located in the periphery of the hexagon. This chapter introduces the concept of functional anatomy. The Couinaud classification defines eight segments, while the Bismuth classification divides the liver into four sectors. The chapter discusses the anatomical abnormalities of the liver. The sinusoidal cells form a functional and histological unit together with the sinusoidal aspect of the hepatocyte. Bile duct epithelial cells line the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and modify the bile derived from the canaliculi of the hepatocytes. Normal liver structure and function depend upon a balance between cell death and regeneration.

results.title: Assessment and characterization of back pain and biopsychosocial influences in lower limb amputation: scoping review.
results.abstract: Back pain affects over half of individuals with lower limb amputation, yet research findings on associated factors remain fragmented. In view of the evolution of pain science in the general population, this fragmentation likely stems from significant variability in the identification, characterization, and classification of pain, as well as inconsistent assessment of associated biopsychosocial factors. This scoping review aims to examine how back pain is currently identified, assessed, classified, and characterized in people with lower-limb amputation, to determine the gaps and inconsistencies that could impede standardization and evidence synthesis. Six electronic databases were searched for studies involving major unilateral acquired lower limb amputation. Two independent reviewers screened articles and extracted data using standardized forms in Covidence. Synthesis focused on identification, classification, reporting of back pain-related biopsychosocial variables, and assessment strategies. Sixty-seven studies were included, predominantly cross-sectional (69%). Although pain intensity was frequently assessed, methods were binary (yes/no), and the use of mechanistic classification and biopsychosocial factors was sparse. Measurement strategies were highly heterogeneous, with standardized frameworks used in only 4 studies. This scoping review reveals a profound discrepancy between contemporary pain science approaches and current pain practice methodologies for the lower limb amputation population. Significant diagnostic gaps persist because of inconsistent classification of pain mechanisms and a void in reporting biopsychosocial variables. Prioritizing standardized frameworks and a population-specific core outcome set is essential to bridge the translational gap. These advancements will improve research quality and facilitate more targeted, evidence-based clinical care for this complex population.

results.title: Astroglial dysfunction in models of CDKL5 deficiency disorder
results.abstract: CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a rare developmental epileptic encephalopathy typically caused by loss of function variants in the gene encoding the X-linked serine–threonine kinase CDKL5. CDKL5 is highly expressed in the brain during development, and key neuronal functions of the kinase include cytoskeletal organisation and synaptic stability. However, at present, little is known about the function of astroglia in CDD. Given the importance of these cells in synaptic development and homeostasis, as well as dysfunction in other epileptic diseases, it was hypothesised that astrocytes may contribute to CDD pathology. Induced pluripotent stem cells harbouring a CDKL5 loss-of-function mutation (and isogenic controls) were derived from CDD patient fibroblasts and differentiated into astrocytes (iAstros). Analysis of iAstros revealed transcriptomic, proteomic and functional dysregulation in CDKL5-mutant iAstros relating to water transport and immunological function, including a diminished response to TNFα stimulation. Moreover, iAstros showed increased branching and reduced phosphorylation of the known CDKL5 target end-binding protein 2 (EB2) - indicative of disrupted cytoskeletal regulation in a manner similar to CDKL5-null neurons. Finally, we report proof-of-concept of novel in vitro models of CDD. CDKL5 was knocked down in adult and foetal human organotypic brain slices through transduction with an AAV encoding a novel CDKL5 shRNA. Slices transduced with the CDKL5 shRNA displayed a trending increase in spontaneous network activity compared to those transduced with a scrambled control, demonstrating the functionality of this model. Importantly, interrogation of these models revealed dysregulation of key astrocytic proteins congruent with the human glial stem cell model. Consequently, this study describes the generation of novel human models of CDD and initial findings of astrocytic dysfunction – paving the way for novel discovery and therapeutic intervention.

results.title: Attitudes to genetic testing and reproductive interventions among patients with inherited retinal disease in Singapore
results.abstract: This study assesses the understanding and attitudes of patients with inherited retinal disease (IRD) towards genetic testing and its application towards reproductive interventions in Singapore. This is a previously uninvestigated group, who may benefit from increased uptake of genetic testing. In this cross-sectional study, patients were recruited via Singapore National Eye Centre (SNEC) and its satellite clinics to answer closed- and open-ended questions about their understanding and attitudes towards genetic testing. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed the adjusted associations between patients’ attitudes towards different applications of genetic testing. Thematic coding and tabulation of frequency were performed for qualitative content analysis. Of 216 participants (median age 57.5 years; 50.9% male, 85.6% Chinese), most had a favorable view of genetic testing (62.5%), and its application to reproductive interventions (preimplantation genetic testing = 56.5%; prenatal testing = 58.8%), despite variable self-reported understanding. Better self-reported understanding was positively associated with support (OR 3.24; 95% CI 1.4, 7.5; p = 0.006), financial coverage (OR 3.29; 95% CI 1.4, 7.9; p = 0.008) and universal availability (OR 4.44; 95% CI 1.8, 10.7; p < 0.001) of genetic testing for patients with IRD. Chinese ethnicity (OR 2.50; 95% CI 1.1, 5.8; p = 0.033), younger age (< 50 years; OR 2.52; 95% CI 1.3, 4.7; p = 0.004), and positive family history (OR 2.03; 95% CI 1.1, 3.8; p = 0.025) were associated with increased support of genetic testing for preimplantation genetic testing. Singaporeans with IRD expressed broad support for genetic testing and its reproductive applications. Education and tailored genetic counselling for patients with poorer levels of understanding could increase uptake and perceived utility of genetic testing.

results.title: Autism: epidemiology, genetics, molecular mechanisms, clinical features, diagnosis, and management
results.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Global prevalence has risen steadily, yet reported rates vary markedly across regions and populations. These discrepancies reflect inequities in diagnostic access and screening capacity rather than true differences in incidence. This review integrates recent advances across the full ASD research spectrum. We first examine global epidemiological patterns and demographic disparities. We then dissect the genetic architecture of ASD, including rare and common variants, copy number variations, and gene-environment interactions that disrupt prenatal and early postnatal brain development. At the molecular level, diverse risk factors converge on shared neurodevelopmental mechanisms. These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory-inhibitory imbalance. We also discuss how these mechanisms manifest in core clinical features, including social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and sensory abnormalities. We summarize current diagnostic standards and their limitations. Cross-species animal models, from Drosophila to non-human primates, are evaluated for their essential roles in mechanistic validation and therapeutic screening. Finally, we assess clinical management strategies, ranging from behavioral and educational interventions to pharmacological and supportive services. By tracing a continuous path from risk factors at the population level through molecular pathophysiology to interventions guided by mechanism, this review offers an integrative synthesis that connects basic discovery to clinical translation. We further discuss how multi-omics and artificial intelligence may advance precise diagnosis rooted in mechanism and personalized treatment.

results.title: Biobank analysis of canine eye disease variants identifies new breed associations and a potential X-linked Retinoschisin 1 disease model
results.abstract: Canine inherited ocular diseases exhibit significant genetic heterogeneity, mirroring many human ophthalmic conditions. This study conducted an extensive screening of 90 OMIA-listed disease-associated variants across 192 affected dogs from 71 breeds to evaluate diagnostic utility and identify novel disease models. This screening identified previously reported variants in 35% of cases, while most cases remained unexplained, prompting whole-genome sequencing of a variant-negative case. This led to the identification of a novel candidate duplication c.442dupC in the X-linked Retinoschisin 1 (RS1) gene, located in the conserved discoidin domain of RS1. If validated, this variant may establish the first spontaneous canine model for human X-linked retinoschisis that may provide a new model for studying pathogenesis and therapeutic approaches. Our analysis also supported the expansion of the known breed distributions for several variants, including progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) variant IFT122 c.3176G>A in Finnish Lapphunds, PRA variant PDE6A c.1847del in Pomeranians, glaucoma variant ADAMTS10 c.1981G>A in East Siberian Laikas, and microphthalmia variant RBP4 c.90_92del in Jack Russell Terriers. The RPGRIP1 c.142_143ins[A[29]; GGAAGCAACAGGATG] PRA variant was observed in four new breeds; however, the reported phenotype was not sufficient to confirm the causative nature. Additionally, our data reclassified the JPH2 c.452A>C PRA variant as a common, benign polymorphism rather than a causal variant in Shih Tzus, emphasizing the need for large-scale genomic validation of published markers. Collectively, these results illustrate the extensive genetic heterogeneity underlying canine eye diseases and underscore the potential for identifying novel preclinical models that advance both veterinary medicine and human vision research.

results.title: Caffeic Acid Regulates High Glucose-Induced Inflammatory Responses in BV-2 Microglial Cells: Implications for Purinergic Signaling
results.abstract: High glucose-induced microglial activation contributes to inflammatory processes associated with diabetic complications. Thus, the effects of caffeic acid (CA) on inflammatory responses and purinergic signaling parameters in high glucose-challenged BV-2 microglial cells were investigated. A) Oxidative stress; b) Enzymatic activities of Ecto-nucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase (E-NTPDase), Ecto-5-nucleotidase (E-5'-NT), and Adenosine deaminase (ADA); c) Density of P2X7R, A1R, and A2AR purinoceptors; d) Inflammatory markers (IBA-1, NLRP3, and IL-1β); and e) Apoptosis and cell cycle were assessed. Treatment with CA (50 and 75 µM, 24 h) in cells exposed to high glucose medium (GL 25 mM, 48 h) increased viability and reduced nitric oxide (NO), reactive species (RS), and thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) levels compared to high glucose-challenged cells. CA also restored ATP and ADP hydrolysis and reduced ADA activity. Furthermore, CA increased the density of the A1R while reversing the high glucose-induced increase in P2X7R and A2AR densities. Moreover, CA treatment attenuated the increase in IL-1β density in high glucose medium, whereas only CA (75 µM) treatment reduced NLRP3 and IBA-1 densities. Besides, this phenolic compound decreased apoptosis and promoted cell cycle progression by increasing the proportion of cells in the S and G2/M phases. Overall, findings suggest that CA attenuates high glucose-induced inflammatory and oxidative alterations in BV-2 microglial cells, besides modulating purinergic enzyme activities and purinoceptor density. These results support the potential involvement of purinergic signaling in the cellular effects of CA and provide possible mechanistic insights into its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions under high glucose conditions.

results.title: Chemoreceptor TRPγ coordinates locomotor activity via regulating intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis in Drosophila
results.abstract: Chemosensation underlies animal behavioral adaptation in ever-changing environments. As a member of the canonical transient receptor potential (TRP), TRPγ orchestrates the chemosensation and the adaptive behavior via fine motor control in Drosophila. Yet, how TRPγ senses and transduces chemical cues has been elusive. Here, we explore cryo-EM structures of dTRPγ in both native and camphor-bound states, with resolutions of 2.18 Å and 3.44 Å, respectively, thereby capturing ligand-induced pore dilation. Through analysis of dTRPγ channel structure, we further identify two allosteric Ca2+-sensing modules: an activating site embedded within the voltage-sensor-like domain (VSLD) and an inhibitory site coordinated by the intracellular ankyrin repeat domain (ARD) and coiled-coil domain (CCD). These spatially segregated sensors convert cytoplasmic Ca2+ into opposing gating signals, maintaining calcium homeostasis via a dual-feedback manner. In vivo, this bidirectional regulation directly controls locomotor kinematics by modulating stride length and velocity, while mutants with lost Ca2+ regulatory functions exhibit impaired locomotor activity. Together, our findings reveal that dTRPγ acts as an independent ion channel, integrating environmental cues with ionic dynamics to drive adaptive behavior. Chemosensation enables animals to adapt their behavior to changing environments. In this study, the authors demonstrate that the Drosophila TRPγ channel integrates chemical cues with intracellular Ca2+ signals to regulate locomotion through bidirectional Ca2+ - dependent gating.

results.title: Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity in Photoinduced Charge-Separations of Cryptochrome: Potential Role in Magnetoreception
results.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
results.abstract: Abstract Radical-pair-based magnetic compass mechanisms are believed to depend on spin-selective reaction pathways modulated by the Earth’s magnetic field. However, the influence of chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) on the magnetic compass function at the molecular level remains largely unknown. In this study, we address this question by monitoring the electron spin polarization of long-range charge-separated (CS) states in cryptochromes using time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy. Our results reveal a measurable, albeit modest, 8% contribution of CISS to the observed spin polarization in the secondary CS state, while the CISS contribution is less than 6% in the tertiary CS state. We propose that the CISS polarization originates from the twisting rearrangement of an oxidized tryptophan residue. This is consistent with previously reported light-induced conformational changes between the inactive and active states of cryptochromes. Furthermore, model calculations predict that even a minor CISS can generate pronounced anisotropy in the signaling-state yield and impact a preferred yield directionality by breaking the magnetic-field inversion symmetry. Together, these findings suggest that CISS may provide an additional mechanism for directional sensitivity in radical pair-based chemical magnetoreception.

results.title: Comparison of Albino and Pigmented Rat Oxygen-Induced Retinopathy Models: From Vascular to Neural Retinal Changes
results.abstract: Purpose: To compare two commonly used rat models of oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR)-the 50/10 model in Sprague-Dawley rats and the 80/40 model in Long-Evans rats-to identify which more closely reproduces the features of human retinopathy. Methods: Dams and pups were exposed from postnatal day 0 (P0) to P14 to alternating oxygen cycles, followed by analyses at P14, P18, and P28. The 50/10 protocol alternated 50% and 10% oxygen every 24 hours, whereas the 80/40 protocol alternated 80% and 40% oxygen every 12 hours. The vascular, structural, and functional retinal changes were assessed using in vivo imaging and electrophysiology, as well as ex vivo histological and molecular analyses. Results: Both OIR protocols induced significant retinal vascular abnormalities compared with controls, but with marked differences in onset, severity, and persistence. The 50/10 protocol produced earlier and more sustained vascular alterations, including reduced vascular coverage, increased vascular tortuosity, and neovascularization beginning at P14. Similar vascular changes appeared later and were less persistent in the 80/40 model. Retinal thinning occurred in both models; however, long-term photoreceptor segment thinning was observed only in the 50/10 protocol. The 50/10 protocol was associated with increased retinal cell death, significant cone photoreceptor loss, and mostly reduced electroretinographic responses, findings that were not observed in the 80/40 protocol. Conclusions: Both OIR models replicate features of human pathology, but differ in disease dynamics. These differences should be considered when selecting an OIR protocol, depending on whether vascular pathology or neurodegeneration is the primary therapeutic target.

results.title: Defining cell type-specific diurnal gene expression in the mouse retina
results.abstract: The mammalian retina exhibits daily oscillations in gene expression that contribute to retinal physiology and visual function. However, the extent to which these temporal patterns differ among retinal cell types remains incompletely understood. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing in the mouse retina over the day and night, identifying rhythmic genes in the six major retinal cell types. Distinct diurnal gene expression patterns across photoreceptors, interneurons, retinal ganglion cells, and Muller glia correspond to their diverse functions across the light cycle. Even core circadian clock genes exhibited differences in paralog expression and rhythmicity across the retina. In contrast, dopamine signaling via the DRD4 receptor is highly rhythmic across most retinal cell types, suggesting dopamine signaling may be a key rhythmicity cue in the retina under diurnal conditions. This dataset highlights the complexity of daily transcriptional regulation in the retina and provides a resource to explore cell-type-specific diurnal rhythms.
